title: Those who love
hook: Guru Gobind Singh: only those who love find the Lord (Tav-Prasad Savaiye)
carry: wealth can be held without love

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was maitra, friendly to all, in Krishna's portrait of the devotee. Your line was a stranger at a bus stop. Today, a Sikh voice on love.

Kings on elephants hung with gold. Armies in polished armor, horses dancing. Ascetics who've stood in cold rivers and gone without food. Pilgrims who've bathed at every holy place. A Sikh hymn walks you through a procession like that. Then, after all that spectacle, the poet stops and says, in effect: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen. Only those who love have found the Lord. The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru.
screen: `KINGS ON ELEPHANTS.` → `ASCETICS IN COLD RIVERS.` → `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: The verses are the Tav-Prasad Savaiye, by Guru Gobind Singh, part of Nitnem, the Sikh daily prayers said in the morning. They look at power, wealth and hard religious effort, one after another. Then comes the line the whole hymn leans on. In the original, in the old Braj language written in Gurmukhi, it begins sach kahon, I speak the truth. Then, in paraphrase: listen, everyone, only those who have loved have found the Lord. Jin prem kio, those who loved, tin hi prabh paio, they alone found God. The word for love there is prem. Notice what the line doesn't say. It doesn't call kings and ascetics bad, or mock pilgrimage. It says none of those, by itself, is the thing. Wealth can be held without love. Even fasting and cold baths can be done without love. The measure is not what you did, but whether you loved. And this love isn't soft. Guru Gobind Singh is remembered as a warrior-saint, who founded the Khalsa and stood against tyranny: a leader who knew armies firsthand, telling everyone that armies aren't what finds God. In Sikh teaching, love is the way to God, and it shows in remembering God's name, honest work and sharing with others.
screen: `THE HYMN AND ITS PARADE.` · `SACH KAHON: THE TURN.` · `WHAT THE LINE DOESN'T SAY.` · `LOVE THAT ISN'T SOFT.` · then, large: `THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing to love with your whole heart, a person, the breath, the light in the room, the simple fact of being alive, and give it everything until the bell. When your mind drifts to plans or worries, the parade going by, come back to the one thing; loving here means returning. If you pray, you can bring a name of God from your own tradition into this.
Prem. The word Guru Gobind Singh uses for love in the Tav-Prasad Savaiye: only those who have it have found the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: wealth can be held without love. The Guru's measure is whether you loved. Day eight hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tav-Prasad Savaiye as part of Nitnem, the daily morning prayers, and the verses are also recited when the Khalsa initiation is given.

chat.says: What's the point of that Sikh hymn that lists kings, armies and pilgrims?
options: After all that display, it says only those who have loved have found God.
It says kings and pilgrims are bad and should all be avoided.
It praises them as the surest ways to find God.
chat.meaning: The hymn's turn is jin prem kio, tin hi prabh paio: only those who have loved have found the Lord.

notes: The original line (sach kahon sun leho sabhai, jin prem kio tin hi prabh paio) is given in transliteration; a Sikh Keeper should confirm the spelling and which savaiya it is.
The 'parade' summary (kings on elephants, armies, ascetics in cold rivers, pilgrims) is drawn from several of the savaiye; confirm it fairly represents the hymn.
'Founded the Khalsa' and recitation at Khalsa initiation (Amrit Sanchar) are standard but should be confirmed.
'Remembering God's name, honest work and sharing with others' summarizes naam japna, kirat karni, vand chhakna; confirm.
Macauliffe 1909 has a translation of these verses, but the exact wording was not certain, so it is paraphrased.
Editor: fixed the gloss 'those who made love' to 'those who loved'; varied the hook opener; softened 'Sikhs recite' to naming Nitnem; removed 'two minutes' from the practice.

Audit: the Tav-Prasad Savaiye are in Braj (written in Gurmukhi), not Punjabi; teach and original note corrected. 'One of the Sikh Gurus' is now 'the tenth Sikh Guru'; the practice no longer says 'for the length of this sit' twice.
